tagline: From the Azrieli towers to the sea, through the White City
lines: In 1909, 66 families split a sand dune into plots by drawing seashells in a lottery.
The town began as Ahuzat Bayit and took the name Tel Aviv in 1910, from Herzl's novel.
The White City holds over 4,000 International Style buildings, mostly from the 1930s.
White walls, deep balconies and raised pillars were all designed to beat the summer heat.
Israel's independence was declared in 1948 in Meir Dizengoff's old house on Rothschild.
Patrick Geddes drew the city's street plan in the 1920s, inspired by the garden city idea.
Hebrew speakers once coined a verb for strolling down Dizengoff Street: l'hizdangef.
The three finished Azrieli towers are a circle, a triangle and a square.
Sarona was founded by German Templers in 1871; some houses were moved, not torn down.
HaKirya has been the army's headquarters since 1948, a footbridge away from Azrieli.
Neve Tzedek, from 1887, was the first Jewish neighbourhood built outside Jaffa's walls.
The old port opened in 1938, closed in 1965, and is now a boardwalk of shops and bars.
Three of Israel's major banks have their headquarters on Yehuda HaLevi Street.
The city's coast runs about 14 km; its first seaside promenade was built in the 1930s.
known_for: cafe culture on Rothschild and Dizengoff
history: 1925: Patrick Geddes draws the master plan
2003: White City named a UNESCO site

neighbourhoods.name: Sarona
neighbourhoods.mood: restored Templer houses, gardens, upscale restaurants and a food market

neighbourhoods.name: White City / Rothschild
neighbourhoods.mood: white Bauhaus blocks and a shady boulevard of cafes and bike lanes

neighbourhoods.name: Dizengoff
neighbourhoods.mood: shops, cafes and bridal stores along the city's old promenade street

neighbourhoods.name: Kerem HaTeimanim
neighbourhoods.mood: tight Yemenite lanes by the Carmel Market, quiet on Shabbat

neighbourhoods.name: Neve Tzedek
neighbourhoods.mood: the oldest quarter: low houses, dance at Suzanne Dellal, boutiques

neighbourhoods.name: Old North
neighbourhoods.mood: leafy, roomy residential blocks from the 1940s and 1950s

neighbourhoods.name: Tel Aviv Port
neighbourhoods.mood: wavy seaside boardwalk with shops, restaurants and nightclubs

neighbourhoods.name: HaKirya
neighbourhoods.mood: army headquarters behind walls, with office towers to the south

streets.Menachem Begin: PM Menachem Begin; was Petah Tikva Road until 2001. Runs past Azrieli and the Kirya
streets.Yigal Alon: Palmach commander Yigal Allon; a spine of office towers in the business district
streets.Ibn Gabirol: Medieval poet Solomon ibn Gabirol; runs past City Hall and Rabin Square
streets.Yitzhak Sadeh: Palmach commander Yitzhak Sadeh; once Bridge Street, as it crosses the Ayalon
streets.HaShalom: 'Peace Road'; a main eastern way in, over the Ayalon by HaShalom station and Azrieli
streets.Sderot Rothschild: Baron Edmond de Rothschild, backer of Jewish settlement; home of Independence Hall
streets.Moshe Dayan: Defence minister Moshe Dayan; once Victory Road, a north-south artery in the southeast
streets.La Guardia: Fiorello La Guardia, New York mayor 1934-45; main street of Yad Eliyahu
streets.Arlosoroff: Labour leader Chaim Arlosoroff, murdered in 1933; runs from the sea to the Ayalon
streets.Herbert Samuel: Herbert Samuel, first British High Commissioner; the seafront road lined with hotels
streets.Dizengoff: Meir Dizengoff, the first mayor; once called Tel Aviv's Champs-Elysees
streets.HaYarkon: The Yarkon River; runs behind the beach past big hotels and most of the embassies
streets.Yehuda HaLevi: Medieval poet Yehuda HaLevi; one of the five first streets, now the banks' street
streets.Shaul HaMelekh: King Saul; passes the Museum of Art and the courts along the Kirya's north wall
streets.Sderot David Ben Gurion: PM David Ben-Gurion (Keren Kayemet until 1974); his house is on it, by Rabin Square
streets.Weizmann: Chaim Weizmann, first President; passes Ichilov Hospital and Kikar HaMedina
streets.Derekh Namir: Mayor Mordechai Namir; once Haifa Road, the main way into the city from the north

food: hummus and falafel on almost every corner
spices and dried fruit at Levinsky Market
rhythm: Sunday to Thursday the roads jam from about 7 to 9 and 5 to 7, and the Ayalon is worst in the morning, while cafes on Rothschild and Dizengoff stay full all day. Friday morning is market and shopping time, then buses stop and shops close for Shabbat until Saturday evening, and the beach fills with drums, barbecues and matkot. Clubs only get going around midnight and run until morning, with the promenade still busy at 4 am in summer.
